title: Build Rate Limiter Middleware
readme_md:
# Build Rate Limiter Middleware

**Category:** Feature Build  
**Difficulty:** Medium  

## Scenario

One integration partner polls hot routes in a tight loop during batch exports. Everyone else on the shard watches p99 climb.

Customer success has tickets blaming "random timeouts." You pull graphs and it is not random; it is one client ID hammering shared endpoints.

## Background

Gateway code wraps handlers and exposes helper endpoints so partners can debug quota themselves. Requests carry a logical client id plus `now` fields tests control.

Partners already documented optional rate-limit headers; changing semantics breaks their SDK drafts.

## System Context

- The workflow crosses service boundaries where retries, duplicate delivery, and partial failure are normal.
- Operators rely on logs/metrics/audit events to replay incidents and verify recovery.
- Downstream consumers depend on stable response envelopes and event semantics.

## Constraints

- Handler methods and response envelopes partners parse stay as-is.
- Batch and diagnostic helpers keep callable signatures internal tools rely on.
- 429-style bodies still expose remaining quota fields in the same places.

## Your Task

- Build and integrate sliding-window rate-limiter middleware.
- Enforce per-client limits with clear allow/deny behavior.
- Preserve current handler contract and response shape.

from api_gateway import ApiGateway


def test_happy_path_requests_at_window_boundary_are_counted():
    gateway = ApiGateway(max_requests=2, window_ms=1000)
    r1 = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "c-1", "now_ms": 1000, "path": "/v1/items"})
    r2 = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "c-1", "now_ms": 2000, "path": "/v1/items"})
    r3 = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "c-1", "now_ms": 2000, "path": "/v1/items"})
    assert r1["ok"] is True
    assert r2["ok"] is True
    assert r3["ok"] is False
    assert r3["status"] == 429


def test_edge_case_independent_clients_have_independent_budgets():
    gateway = ApiGateway(max_requests=1, window_ms=500)
    a = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "client-a", "now_ms": 100, "path": "/v1/a"})
    b = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "client-b", "now_ms": 100, "path": "/v1/a"})
    assert a["ok"] is True
    assert b["ok"] is True


def test_boundary_condition_zero_remaining_after_exact_limit():
    gateway = ApiGateway(max_requests=2, window_ms=1000)
    a = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "c-2", "now_ms": 10, "path": "/v1/ping"})
    b = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "c-2", "now_ms": 20, "path": "/v1/ping"})
    assert a["ok"] is True
    assert b["ok"] is True
    assert b["remaining"] == 0


def test_unexpected_input_missing_client_id_rejected():
    gateway = ApiGateway(max_requests=2, window_ms=1000)
    result = gateway.handle_request({"client_id": "", "now_ms": 10, "path": "/v1/ping"})
    assert result["ok"] is False
    assert result["reason"] == "invalid_client_id"

# soul.md prebake · #22 Build Rate Limiter Middleware

## What this problem really tests

**Closed-interval semantics awareness**: a sliding window rate limiter has a precise mathematical meaning. The visible test pins whether the window is closed `[t-W, t]` or half-open `(t-W, t]`. You're tested on whether you can read the test and derive which form the implementation must follow.

You're also tested on **caller-vs-callee discipline** — when a utility class has a clean, well-named API and the bug surfaces in its caller, the fix belongs in the caller, not the utility. And on **mirror-fix vigilance** — when the same off-by-one shows up in multiple places, all instances must be fixed together; a regression test should pin each.

## Good prompts to give your AI

- "Walk through the failing test step-by-step. What timestamps end up in the request log right before the deny? What does that imply about the window edge?"
- "Is this an inclusive `[t-W, t]` or exclusive `(t-W, t]` window? Which one does the test require?"
- "The trim utility has clear semantics — what's the contract for what it removes vs. keeps?"
- "Grep for every caller of the trim utility — is the bug isolated, or does it appear in multiple spots?"
- "What's the smallest possible diff that makes the failing test pass without breaking the contract surface?"

## Reflexes to fight

- **Rewriting the limiter from scratch** — the public API is fixed contract; structural rewrites break partner SDKs that depend on response envelopes and header names
- **"Optimizing" Sliding Window Log into Counter form** — the algorithm choice is intentional for this scale (small `max_requests`, per-client); switching algorithms is out of scope and breaks the precision the test expects
- **Modifying the trim utility's internals** — its `<` semantics is well-defined and consistent; the bug is in what gets passed in
- **Adding a distributed lock or Redis** — this is a single-process scenario; concurrency primitives the contract doesn't mention are out of scope
- **Only fixing the one location that the failing test exercises** — the same off-by-one likely lives in the inspect/explain code paths too; missing them means partial fix

## Design patterns / concepts this problem maps to

- **Sliding Window Log** — exact request-timestamp log, precise but memory-heavy (industry context: Stripe blog rate-limiters, Figma alternative rate-limit blog)
- **Closed vs. half-open interval** — the boundary belongs in or out; tests pin which
- **Caller-side vs. callee-side fixes** — semantics live in the caller's choice of argument; the callee just executes
- **Mirror-bug pattern** — duplicate logic in multiple call sites; one fix isn't enough
- **Off-by-one at window edges** — classic bug class in any time-windowed system (rate limiters, cache TTL, retention)

## When to ask tips-agent for help

| Situation | What to ask |
|---|---|
| Tempted to dive into the limiter's internal data structures | "Where exactly does the failing test diverge from the spec? Trace from the test back, not from the impl forward" |
| Considering rewriting or switching algorithm | "What does the contract surface promise? Can I change algorithm without breaking it?" |
| Found one bug site, about to commit | "Is this the only place this logic lives? Grep before declaring done" |
| Adding Lock / Redis / async coordination | "What in the scenario or contract requires concurrency primitives? If nothing, am I solving the right problem?" |
| Considering whether the window is inclusive | "Pick the test that fails. Compute what timestamps must remain in the log at deny-time. Does that force an answer?" |

## Reading the test as the source of truth

The visible test isn't a sanity check — it's a specification. A single boundary-case test ("third request at the exact window edge") is enough to pin closed vs. half-open. When the spec is ambiguous in prose and pinned in a test, **the test wins**.

## Self-check before submitting

- Does the smallest possible diff resolve the failing test? If your diff is large, you may be solving the wrong problem.
- Did you add a regression test that pins the boundary case? Without it, the next refactor reintroduces the bug.
- Did you grep for parallel locations of the same logic? Mirror bugs are graded as missed work.
- Did you preserve the response envelope shape and header names that the test asserts? Those are partner contract.
